1.pericope_label: Isaac resolves to bless Esau, and Rebekah overhears

schools.summary: Gill puts Isaac near a hundred and thirty-seven, notes that this was Ishmael's age at death and may have set him thinking of his own, and records that Rebekah may have overheard the charge or, as the Targum has it, learned of it by the Holy Spirit. Calvin raises the whole transaction above a family matter: the blessing was no mere prayer but a legitimate sanction divinely interposed to make the grace of election manifest, so that Isaac stood there as a prophet and interpreter of God rather than as a father or private person, and God's permitting him to be deceived proves that Jacob was not raised by any human will. He observes that Isaac's attachment to Esau was a blindness hindering him more than the dimness of his eyes, and on Rebekah holds both ends at once — her stratagem was faulty and sinned the more grievously in sporting with wiles in a sacred matter, darkening the oracle she trusted, yet her readiness to provoke her husband and risk her favourite son could have sprung from nothing but faith, a pure knowledge not always so governing the pious that they never slide while holding the right course.

Henry reckons Isaac about a hundred and thirty-five and allows him the charitable reading, that he was not knowing, or not understanding, or not duly considering the oracle, and was governed by natural affection and the usual course of settlements more than he should have been; from this he draws that we take our measures from our own reason rather than from revelation, expecting the promise to fall to the mighty and noble, though God does not see as man sees. He adds that parents justly offended at their children must not be implacable, that the uncertainty of our departure should quicken us to do the work of life while it is day, and that prayer is the work of the soul and not of the lips only, a blessing not reaching the heart unless it comes from the heart.

Clarke makes Isaac a hundred and seventeen, calling the higher figure the received opinion and rejecting it, and attributes the failing eyesight to the affliction from which he afterwards recovered. He would have guessed a shield for the disputed hunting implement had the Greek and Latin not made it a quiver, and flatly rejects the derivation of our word hanger from the Hebrew, since that word entered English only after the Crusades and came from a Persian name for a dagger. On the meat he argues that the blessing was a divine right requiring appropriate ceremony, no covenant being reckoned binding unless the parties had eaten together, so that Isaac could not convey the right until he had eaten what the receiver provided. Of Rebekah he is hardest, observing that some claim a divine intimation for her but that one so instructed would not have needed deceit, and that she took the most exceptionable means available. Wesley repeats Henry on Isaac's design and on prayer as the work of the soul.

Ellicott sets out the chapter's stakes, that an election had to be declared as between Ishmael and Isaac, but that where Abraham obeyed with a heavy heart Isaac struggled against God's will and had his assent extracted by craft; he contrasts Esau, brave and vigorous but caring for nothing beyond earthly things, with Jacob, sedentary and calculating yet valuing what Esau despised, and distributes the blame evenly between the artifices of Rebekah and Jacob and Isaac's attempt to annul a plain prophecy. He makes Isaac a hundred and seventeen with sixty-three years still to live, and remarks that the word old is used so loosely in these books that Samuel is called old when at most middle-aged. On the hunting implement he concludes from its root that it was something like our hanger, a sort of knife, while allowing that the Targum and Syriac read a sword and that nothing certain can be said; and he notes that an Arab sheikh's rare dish of flesh is dressed with almonds, pistachios and raisins, so that a kid would not easily be told from an antelope. Keil and Delitzsch judge Isaac severely, since he held to his preference without regard to the words spoken before the birth and took no notice of Esau's bartered birthright or his Canaanite marriages, the infirmity of his flesh appearing in his wish to have his spirits raised by a dish of venison.

debates: How old Isaac was at this time. Gill and Henry put him near a hundred and thirty-five, Gill supporting it by Ishmael's age at death; Clarke and Ellicott make him a hundred and seventeen, Clarke naming and rejecting the higher figure as merely the received opinion. All agree he outlived the scene by more than forty years.

What the disputed hunting implement was. Ellicott derives it from a root meaning to hang and compares our word hanger, a sort of knife, while noting that the Targum and Syriac read a sword; Clarke rejects that comparison outright, since hanger entered English only after the Crusades from a Persian word for a dagger, and would himself have guessed a shield but for the Greek and Latin versions.

How far Rebekah is culpable. Clarke leaves her nothing to plead and calls her means the most exceptionable available; Ellicott lays the first fault on Isaac and allows that she may have thought herself preventing a wrong; Calvin condemns the deceit as sporting with wiles in a sacred matter while insisting that only faith could have moved her to risk so much.
outliers: Clarke's note that the English word hanger postdates the Crusades and derives from a Persian name for a dagger, so that it cannot be used to explain the Hebrew.
Ellicott's observation that an Arab sheikh's flesh is dressed with almonds and pistachios, so that a kid could easily pass for an antelope.
Calvin's judgment that Isaac's attachment to his elder son was a blindness that hindered him more than the dimness of his eyes.
Ellicott's remark that old is so loose a term in these books that Samuel is called old when he was at most middle-aged.
themes: a will made in the dark
the elder shall serve the younger
a hunting weapon of unknown kind
faith mixed with contrivance

6.pericope_label: Rebekah’s plan, and the disguising of Jacob

schools.summary: Gill reports the Targum's turn on Rebekah's answer, that it had been revealed to her in prophecy that no curse would fall on her son, and takes her words for strong faith in the oracle; he notes that Jacob obeyed his mother rightly so far as fetching the kids went. Calvin calls Jacob's hesitation very contrary to faith, since a man who debates with himself shows himself deficient, and adds a second error, that he dreaded his father's anger rather than reverencing God, holding that a right end does not make an oblique course lawful; yet he insists faith prevailed, since Jacob preferred a bare and seemingly empty benediction to his present quiet and to life itself, and even his fear of his father sprang from the true fear of God. Of Rebekah he says she sins again, burning with a zeal so hasty that she never asks how God regards it and, having no command, takes her own counsel, though the zeal sprang from reverence for God's word; his strongest argument is from Balaam, that a Spirit which forced blessing from a venal tongue could far more easily have turned the tongue of Isaac.

Henry draws up a balance sheet: the end was good, since Rebekah had the oracle to direct her, but the means were bad and in no way justifiable, wronging Isaac by taking advantage of his infirmity, wronging Jacob by teaching him to deceive, and leaving him open to endless scruples since the blessing might be revoked as given by mistake of the person. He sets out the honest course she might have taken instead and thinks Isaac would probably have been prevailed on to bless Jacob knowingly, concluding that God left her to herself so that he might have the glory of bringing good out of evil. He observes that Providence has so ordered features that no two faces are alike, without which variety commerce could scarcely be carried on, and that Esau must have been rough indeed if nothing less than kid-skins would serve to counterfeit him.

Clarke notes that the spirit of the law against making the blind wander was understood even in those early times, and that Jacob seems at this moment to have had a more tender conscience than his mother; he calls the Targum's paraphrase of Rebekah's answer curious and her undertaking a dreadful responsibility, and lays down the principle that the sacred writer states the facts as they were but nowhere says any man should copy them, often relating what he never recommends. On the garments he reports Ainsworth's argument that they were holy robes, since the priest under the law had garments to minister in, asking why else Esau's own wives did not keep them rather than his mother, who stored them in sweet chests against moths. Wesley reproduces Henry's argument about the good end and the bad means closely.

Ellicott notes that Rebekah's report of the charge adds the covenant name and defends her against the charge of inventing it, since only the main sense of Isaac's words is recorded, adding that the phrase meant more to Jacob than to Esau, who valued the blessing chiefly for its temporal benefits; he reckons two kids about equal to one antelope and expects the occasion to have been marked by a feast. He observes that no curse in fact followed, Isaac afterwards acknowledging the substantial justice of the act and confirming the blessing, yet finds it strange that neither mother nor son scrupled at the immorality, apparently thinking a right end justified falsehood. On the raiment he supposes the elder son held a sort of priestly office and ministered at sacrifices for his failing father, reasoning that ordinary clothing would not have been kept in the mother's tent; and on the skins he cautions that oriental goats are famous for soft silky wool whereas hair on a man's body is never of a delicate texture.

debates: Whether a good end excuses the means. Henry judges the end good and the means indefensible, and thinks a plain appeal to Isaac would probably have succeeded; Ellicott finds it strange that neither mother nor son scrupled, while noting that no curse followed and that Isaac later owned the substantial justice of the act; Calvin denies that the truth of God was to be aided by falsehood and argues from Balaam that the Spirit could have turned Isaac's tongue without any deceit.

What the goodly raiment was. Clarke follows Ainsworth in taking it for holy robes used in ministering, on the ground that common clothes would have stayed with Esau's own household; Ellicott reaches the same conclusion by a different route, supposing a priestly office in the firstborn and noting that ordinary raiment would not be stored in the mother's tent.

What Jacob's hesitation shows. Calvin makes it a proof of deficient faith compounded by a fear of man rather than of God, yet traces even that fear back to a true valuation of the grace at stake; Clarke reads it as a conscience more tender than his mother's; Henry as a just dread of the curse pronounced on those who mislead the blind.
outliers: Calvin's argument from Balaam, that a Spirit which forced blessing out of a venal tongue could far more easily have turned the tongue of a willing Isaac.
Clarke's principle that the sacred writer states facts as they were and often relates what he nowhere recommends.
Ellicott's caution that oriental goat hair is soft and silky while hair on a man's body is not, which is why rough skins were needed for the disguise.
Henry's observation that Providence has so ordered human features that no two faces are exactly alike.
themes: a good end by a lie
a curse taken on another’s head
borrowed clothes
the elder brother’s garments

18.pericope_label: Jacob before his father, and the blessing given

schools.summary: Gill draws a finer line than the rest, allowing that Jacob might have been excused had he claimed only the birthright, which he had bought, but holding that his saying he was Esau admits no defence; Calvin marks the change of nerve, that a man timid and anxious at first now lies confidently, which teaches that one who has passed the bounds of duty soon allows himself unmeasured license; he faces the awkwardness that the blessing seems void for want of faith in the man who gave it, and answers that God performed his work by Isaac's hand without making the instrument a willing party, as pastors reconcile men to God by his command yet cannot discern where their seed will bear. He is content with the allegory of Ambrose, that the younger is blessed under the person of the elder in borrowed garments whose odour pleases the father, as we are blessed entering God's presence in the name of Christ; and he insists that the words are not wishes but promises, Isaac speaking as the authorised interpreter of God.

Henry marvels that so plain a man could play the part, concludes that lying is soon learnt, and counts the untruths — that he was Esau, that he had done as his father bade him, that the dish was venison, and worst of all that he fathered the speed of it upon God — declaring the whole written not for imitation but for admonition, since good men have failed in the very graces for which they were most eminent. He turns the moment of doubt into a figure, the voice being Jacob's and the hands Esau's, which is the picture of a hypocrite who speaks like a saint and works like a sinner, the judgment going by the hands. He sorts the blessing under three heads — plenty, with heaven and earth concurring; power, and dominion over his brethren; and a standing with God, whose friendship and enmity should follow his own — and holds that more is comprised in it than appears, since it entails the promise of the Messiah and of the church.

Clarke will allow no palliation, reporting Calmet's division of the fraud into words, actions and clothing, and objecting that men have laboured not merely to excuse Rebekah and Jacob but to show the whole thing was according to the mind of God. He attributes Isaac's failure to detect the disguise to illness, since a man who cannot tell a kid's hide from his son's arm has a sense of feeling much impaired; he supposes aromatic herbs laid up with the clothes, a custom still kept where thyme and lavender are put in wardrobes, sprigs laid in eastern manuscripts against worms, and Russia leather carried among clothes to the Indies; and following Bishop Newton he divides the matter so that in temporal advantages the brothers were to be much alike, while the promise of the blessed seed could be given to one only. Wesley follows Henry throughout, on the lying, on the kiss and the praise, and on the three heads of the blessing.

Ellicott finds two things that roused Isaac's suspicion — the game came back too quickly, since it had to be sought far from the pastures, and the answer about providence was not in Esau's way of thinking, so that Jacob broke character — and adds that the twins' voices, though somewhat alike, had their peculiarities and that Isaac caught the difference, though the kid-skins fitted cleverly and the doubt vanished at a touch. He corrects the notion that Isaac was bedridden, since he is bidden to arise and sit, and notes that the Hebrews sat at meals until they learned reclining from the Romans. He observes that the pastures of Palestine are fragrant with aromatic plants and suspects Isaac meant to contrast a life in the open field with the odour of the cattle-shed; that the divine name shifts where dew and fat places are in view, the God of nature being properly invoked; that Isaac stops short of the greater promise that in him all families should be blessed, for which he offers three reasons. Keil and Delitzsch note that Isaac's direct question was put in order to be rid of the suspicion the voice had raised.

debates: How far Jacob's words admit of excuse. Gill would excuse the claim to the birthright, which had been bought, but not the claim to be Esau; Clarke refuses all palliation and objects to those who make the whole affair God's will; Calvin counts three direct falsehoods and sees in them a man losing all restraint; Henry declares the record written for admonition and not imitation.

Why Isaac's suspicion was allayed. Ellicott credits the neat fit of the kid-skins after the voice had already betrayed a difference; Clarke lays it to a sense of feeling impaired by illness; Henry to a man unable to trust his ears against his hands.

Why the blessing stops short of the promise that in him all families should be blessed. Ellicott offers three reasons — that such a gift is God's and not man's, that Isaac doubted Esau's worthiness, or that his own wrong conduct narrowed his sight; Clarke, after Newton, divides temporal parity between the brothers from a spiritual promise given to one only; Calvin complains that nothing heavenly is named at all.
outliers: Ellicott's observation that Jacob broke character by seeing providence in a successful hunt, which was not Esau's way of thinking.
Henry's figure of the hypocrite whose voice is Jacob's and whose hands are Esau's, the judgment going by the hands.
Clarke's note on aromatic herbs kept in wardrobes and laid in eastern manuscripts against worms, and on Russia leather carried among clothes to the Indies.
Calvin's comparison of Isaac to a pastor who scatters seed at God's command without discerning where the fruit will fall.
themes: a plain man learns to lie
the voice and the hands
a field the Lord has blessed
what the blessing did not say

30.pericope_label: Esau returns too late, and receives what is left

schools.summary: Gill lists four causes of Isaac's trembling at once — Jacob's craft, Esau's loss, his own act against his own intention, and an overruling providence bringing the thing about exactly as the oracle said, which he thinks may only now have come fresh into Isaac's mind — and notes that the Targums and Jarchi soften the word for Jacob's subtlety into wisdom, whether excusing or commending the act, while insisting that the word means fraud and suspecting Isaac used it partly to clear himself with Esau. Calvin says the faith long smothered in Isaac shines out and emits fresh sparks, the fear itself springing from faith; he refuses to soften Esau's tears, which he calls desperation rather than piety, entering by no gate of faith and asking a second blessing as though his father could breathe them out indiscriminately, and he finds no penitence in a man who accuses his brother and takes no blame himself. He then sets the works of the two side by side and finds Esau the better — obedient, labouring, and speaking nothing but truth — concluding that what Jacob obtained was a free gift and nothing earned; and he observes that none of the closing prophecy was fulfilled in Esau himself, Jacob having tendered his brother obedience on the way home, so that it looked past both men to their posterity.

Henry calls Esau's cry a great and exceedingly bitter one that made his father's tent ring, and notes that the man who had made light of the birthright now found no place of repentance though he sought it carefully with tears.

Clarke prefers the marginal rendering, that Isaac trembled with a great trembling greatly, and takes it for the deep concern of a man who sees how he has been deceived; he allows Esau to call the old sale a robbery, since Jacob had taken advantage of a perishing man; and, again following Bishop Newton, he takes the sword in Esau's blessing to mean not perpetual war but a fierce temper living by hunting and raid. Wesley adds that men who follow their affections rather than the divine will involve themselves in just such perplexities, and supposes Isaac either recollected the oracle or felt himself unusually filled with the Spirit while blessing, so that he perceived God saying Amen to it; he reads Esau's grant as real but inferior, noting that dew stands first in Jacob's blessing and fatness first in Esau's according to what each valued most, and that Esau would gain some power but never dominion over his brother.

Ellicott denies that Isaac's trembling was vexation at being deceived, holding that what he felt was that he had been resisting God, the proof being that he persists no longer, has no word of blame for Rebekah or Jacob, and confirms the blessing outright. He observes that Esau's play on his brother's name has been a lasting revenge, the bad sense he first put upon it having stuck ever since, though the word properly means one who follows close upon another's heels; he limits the inheritance to one son, so that Esau must be content with some mitigation of his lot; and on the closing blessing he reports that most modern expositors take the preposition the other way, so that Esau's dwelling shall be away from and not of the fat places of the earth, calls the familiar rendering of the last clause scarcely more than a guess by two or three old Jewish commentators since the word means to toss the yoke, and traces Edom's history through its long dependency on Judah, its revolts under Joram and Ahaz, and its reconquest by Hyrcanus.

debates: Whether Esau's dwelling was to be of or away from the fat places of the earth. Ellicott reports most modern expositors for the second, which turns the promise into a deprivation; Wesley and Clarke read the words as a real if inferior grant, Wesley contrasting the order in which dew and fatness stand in the two blessings.

What Isaac's trembling meant. Clarke makes it the concern of a man who sees he has been deceived; Gill multiplies its causes to four, including the providence that fulfilled the oracle; Ellicott denies vexation altogether and makes it the discovery that he had been resisting God; Calvin calls it faith emitting fresh sparks, the fear springing from faith itself.

How Esau's conduct in this scene weighs. Calvin notes that on works Esau shows the better of the two, obeying, labouring and speaking only truth, yet finds no penitence in him, since he accuses his brother and takes no blame himself; Henry stresses that he found no place of repentance though he sought it with tears; Ellicott sees him take a lasting revenge in his pun.
outliers: Calvin's observation that, judged by their works in this scene, Esau shows the better of the two brothers — obedient, labouring, and speaking nothing but the truth.
Ellicott's remark that Esau's pun on his brother's name was a lasting revenge, fixing a bad sense on the word ever after.
Ellicott's report that the familiar rendering of Esau's last clause is scarcely more than a guess by two or three old Jewish commentators, the word meaning to toss the yoke.
Wesley's contrast that dew stands first in Jacob's blessing and fatness first in Esau's, according to what each man valued most.
themes: a trembling that was faith
a cry too late
a name turned into a taunt
a blessing away from the fat places

41.pericope_label: Esau’s hatred, and Jacob sent away

schools.summary: Gill notes what Esau actually grudged — a better country, greater plenty and dominion — the promise of the Messiah being no concern of his; he leaves open whether Rebekah learned of the threat by revelation, as the rabbis say, or from one of Esau's confidants, as Aben Ezra supposes and he thinks not at all unlikely; he reports the various reckonings of the few days, prefers one or two years, and observes that Jacob in fact stayed twenty, his mother probably dying before he came back, after which she is never mentioned again; and he says she withheld the threat from Isaac lest it bring his grey hairs with sorrow to the grave. Calvin makes Esau's threat worse than murder, since he knew his father was the herald of the benediction and now prepares to abolish a decree of God with the sword; he turns the sharpest edge on Rebekah, who by her own deed had put her son in danger, arguing that mere partiality would have taken the short way of restoring the birthright to Esau and removing the cause of quarrel, so that her refusal proves extraordinary faith; he denies that so mild a man as Jacob endangered his brother and concludes she expected God to avenge the murder and would have been bereaved either way, being forced to dread whichever son survived; and he acquits her of falsehood toward Isaac, since she neither told the whole truth nor left the whole unsaid.

Henry puts Esau in the way of Cain, hating a brother for no reason but that his father blessed him and God loved him, and calls the hatred both causeless and cruel, since nothing less than blood would satisfy it; he wonders how a man could say the word brother and vow his death in the same breath, and observes that the happiness of saints is the envy of sinners.

Clarke explains the timing of the threat by the funeral, at which the sons were always present, recalling that Ishmael came from his own country to help bury Abraham while both brothers in the event buried Isaac with the enmity long since dead; he reports Houbigant's smoother rendering that Esau was meditating the murder but doubts it is the sense of the original, being sure Esau found real pleasure in the prospect; he makes the absence forty years and cites the general opinion of the rabbis that Rebekah died first; he explains the fear of losing both sons in one day by the avenger of blood, who being next of kin would have killed Esau; and he says Rebekah frames a reason for the journey and conceals the true one, doubting whether her stated fear was even real, and warns that those who try to sanctify means by the end compass themselves with their own sparks and lie down in sorrow. Wesley says the murderer would be sacrificed to justice by the magistrate or by God's own hand, and alone refuses to excuse the pretext, calling it more artifice still, since if we use guile once we shall readily use it again — for though a blessing came to Jacob's posterity by his lying, it brought him heavy affliction for many years.

Ellicott explains the timing by the funeral and reports a proposed rendering that would have Esau kill Jacob before the mourning rather than after, rejecting it since the Hebrew gives it no support and it makes utterly inhuman a man who, with all his faults, had a warm heart; he adds a second motive to the flight, that Jacob was now acknowledged heir of the promises and had to conform to the family rule and marry among his kindred, so that the long journey and the parting from his mother came as the immediate fruit of the scheming; and he makes the absence forty years, noting that Isaac lived to see his son return though Rebekah did not, which he still reckons better than that Esau should have killed him and been banished like another Cain. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the phrase for Esau's comforting himself as procuring comfort by retaliation, that is, avenging himself.

debates: How long Jacob was away. Gill makes it twenty years, having first canvassed rabbinic readings of the few days as one year or a few; Clarke and Ellicott both make it forty, Clarke citing the rabbis for Rebekah dying first and Ellicott noting that Isaac lived to see the return though she did not.

Whether Rebekah's excuse to Isaac was a lie. Calvin acquits her, since she neither told the whole truth nor left the whole unsaid, and had reason both to spare her husband and not to inflame Esau; Clarke calls it framing a reason and concealing the true one, and doubts the stated fear was real; Wesley calls it more artifice still and draws the moral that guile once used is readily used again.

What being deprived of both in one day means. Clarke supplies the avenger of blood, who as next of kin would have killed Esau; Wesley has the murderer sacrificed to justice by magistrate or by God's own hand; Calvin denies Jacob was any danger to his brother and concludes that Rebekah looked for God to avenge the murder and would have been bereaved of the survivor by dread and detestation.
outliers: Ellicott's rejection of a proposed rendering that would place the murder before the mourning, on the ground that it makes Esau utterly inhuman when he had a warm heart.
Clarke's explanation that the sons were always present at a father's burial, which is why Esau fixed on that occasion.
Calvin's argument that mere partiality would have restored the birthright to Esau and ended the quarrel, so that Rebekah's refusal to do so proves her faith.
Wesley's observation that though a blessing came to Jacob's posterity through his lying, it brought him heavy affliction for many years after.
themes: a hatred that called him brother
a few days that were forty years
both in one day
guile used twice
